newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire war edges towards Kisangani showdown.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war edges towards Kisangani showdown.

text.p: Rebels trying to take Zaire's garrison city of Kisangani reported skirmishes with government troops in a prelude to what is expected to be the biggest showdown in a five-month civil war.
Rebel radio said the clashes on Tuesday were on approach roads into Kisangani, the immediate object of guerrillas advancing steadily from Zaire's eastern border since October.

Rebels have been predicting the imminent fall of Kisangani for days. Their reports of clashes suggested growing resistance from Zaire's retreating mercenary-backed army, which is making what is widely seen as its last stand in Kisangani.
With fighting once again stirring international concern for refugees trapped for months in the jungle, the United States rejected renewed preassure from France for U.N. intervention.
"We are not prepared right now to sign on to a multi-national force," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

He said U.S. officials would continue to discuss the multi-national force idea, put forward by Secretary-General Kofi Annan and backed by France. But he said Washington believed the political course being pursued at the moment was the right one.

"We think that actually what's being done is the best way to help the refugees and to stop the fighting -- to pursue the ceasefire and to continue to encourage the United Nations to deliver this humanitarian assistance," he said. "We do not believe there is a military solution to the problems of Zaire."
There were new signs that the conflict could take on other international dimensions, on top of an underlying risk of drawing in or spiralling violence into neighbouring states.
U.N. sources and diplomats said Angolan government troops and former UNITA rebels had moved into Zaire in recent weeks with some involved in fighting in the east of the country.
"We have seen troop movements on both sides into Zaire," said a U.N. official who asked not be identified.

The official said UNITA troops had been flown out of bases in UNITA-held territory at Lusamba and Jamba to help the government of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko in its fight against Tutsi-led rebels.
"We think at least 2,000 UNITA troops have been sent to Zaire. Most of these are fighting troops," the U.N. source said.
He said UNITA got involved in the conflict to keep open vital supply routes out of Zaire to its bases in the north and east of Angola.
The role of Angolan government soldiers was not as clear but sources said technical advisers had been sent to assist the Zairean rebels amid hopes of cutting off the UNITA supplies.
Zaire accuses neighbours Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of helping the rebels, a charge they all deny.

The Zairean defence ministry said the army, which has sown land mines round Kisangani, was on a war footing there but rejected suggestions from the rebels that they were within 10 km (six miles) of the city.
"They are around 40 km (25 miles) from Kisangani. We are still on a war footing," a ministry spokesman told Reuters.
The spokesman, however, acknowledged the fall of the port town of Moba on Lake Tanganyika and deep in copper-rich Shaba province, saying rebels seized it on Sunday.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila who wants to end Mobutu's 31-year rule has rejected a U.N. ceasefire call. His forces repeated a Thursday deadline for Zaire troops to lay down their weapons. Mobutu is ailing with cancer in France.
